Module Structure

## Where this module sits

| | |

| **Module** | The Evolution of Machine Learning and AI |

| **Award** | Award Certificate in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Engineering (30 ECTS) |

| **Delivery** | Fully online — live lectures, asynchronous content, self-paced labs |
| **Effort** | 24 lecture hours + 24 practical hours + 87 hours independent learning |

## What you do each week

Every teaching week carries a **2h live online lecture** and a **2h practical lab**, with self-paced
asynchronous content here on Tutors. Twelve teaching weeks are grouped into four three-week sprints,
each closed by a reading week. Two of those sprints close on an assessment rather than new content.

The 87 hours of independent learning is where the module actually happens: reading, running the labs
properly rather than skimming them, and — from Week 10 — building the final-project artefact.

## Learning outcomes

Short forms of the descriptor outcomes. The full wording is in the module descriptor; the mapping of
outcomes to weeks and assessments is in **Constructive Alignment** in the Semester Map.

los.title: Why the Module Looks Like This
los.summary: Rationale behind the structure
los.contentMd:
# Why the Module Looks Like This

Rationale behind the structure

A conventional version of this module would follow the field's textbook chronology and spend three
weeks on classical material before reaching anything current. This one treats history as a **fast
orientation — one week, not three** — and spends the freed time on where the field is actually moving.

Three commitments follow from that.

## 1. Science-inspired AI

Two directions at once. **AI for science**: AlphaFold 3, GNoME materials discovery, weather and
climate models. **Science-grounded architectures**: physics-informed neural networks, neural
operators, neural ODEs, diffusion understood as thermodynamics.

The unifying idea, and the one to carry from Week 4 into Week 5: *embedding scientific structure as
inductive bias makes models more data-efficient and more trustworthy*. An architecture is an
assumption about the world. When the assumption matches reality, the model needs less data and
generalises better.

## 2. Scale-free, lean LLMs

The move beyond brute-force scaling: state-space models such as Mamba, linear and attention-free
architectures, mixture-of-experts, distillation, low-bit quantization, parameter-efficient
fine-tuning, on-device and neuromorphic deployment, and test-time-compute reasoning.

Scaling worked. The module's thesis is that the frontier has moved past it — and that the interesting
engineering question is now *how small and how cheap can this get while still working*.

## 3. Responsible AI from day one

Bias, fairness and explainability sit in **Week 2**, framed as a design constraint that shapes every
model built afterwards, rather than as a closing topic bolted on in Week 11. Moving it early also
means LO6 is taught and consolidated well before the Week 6 quiz.

## Frontier strands beyond the current descriptor

These four strands are additions. If the programme is validated against the existing descriptor, the
descriptor's indicative content — and ideally LOs 2, 3 and 7 — should be refreshed to name them.

| Strand | Week | Examples taught |
|---|---|---|
| Science-grounded architectures | 5 | PINNs, neural operators (FNO, DeepONet), neural ODEs, diffusion as thermodynamics, equivariant/geometric nets, thermodynamics-informed GNNs |
| Scale-free architectures | 8 | State-space models (S4, Mamba, Mamba-2), RetNet, RWKV, linear/attention-free models, mixture-of-experts, test-time-compute reasoning |
| Lean / efficient models | 9 | Distillation (transformer→recurrent), low-bit quantization including 1-bit, pruning, LoRA/QLoRA, small language models, edge/TinyML, neuromorphic/spiking |
| AI for scientific discovery | 11 | AlphaFold 2→3, GNoME materials discovery, protein binder design, weather and climate models, foundation models for science |

los.title: Sprint 1 — Fast Foundations + Responsible AI Up Front
los.contentMd:
# Sprint 1 — Fast Foundations + Responsible AI Up Front

**Weeks 1–3.** History compressed to a single orientation week, ethics installed before anything is
built, and the whole of classical ML and neural network training delivered in one applied week.

## Week 1 — The shape of the field: cycles, breakthroughs, and what the current wave got right

`Indicative 1, 5` · `LO1` · `topic-01-shape-of-the-field`

**Lecture (2h).** A brisk tour of the evolution — pioneers, two winters, resurgence — framed as *why
the field moves in cycles* and what the modern wave actually got right: data, compute and
architecture arriving together. Ends by setting the module thesis: scaling worked, but the frontier is
now moving past brute force toward science-grounded and lean systems.

**Lab (2h).** The AI Evolution Timeline as a 30-minute macro orientation. Then environment setup:
Python, Colab, HuggingFace, Ollama, GitHub.

## Week 2 — Responsible AI, before we build anything

`Indicative 9` · `LO6` · `topic-02-responsible-ai`

**Lecture (2h).** Bias, fairness, accountability, transparency and explainability introduced as a
design constraint rather than an afterthought. Where bias enters: data, objective, deployment.
Documented real-world harms. The EU AI Act and responsible-AI principles read as engineering
requirements. This lens is applied in every subsequent week.

**Lab (2h).** Audit a dataset and a model for biased outcomes with the Bias & Fairness Explorer;
apply explainability tools (SHAP, LIME); watch how moving a decision threshold moves the fairness
metrics.

## Week 3 — How machines learn, fast: classical ML, neural nets, training

`Indicative 2, 3, 7` · `LO2, LO4` · `topic-03-how-machines-learn`

**Lecture (2h).** Compressed but applied: classical ML (regression, trees, SVMs) → the perceptron and
multilayer networks → backpropagation and gradient descent, intuitively → why GPUs and big data
unlocked depth. PyTorch introduced as the working framework.

**Lab (2h).** Train a classical model and a small neural net in PyTorch; use the Gradient Descent
Explorer to see learning-rate effects, convergence and local minima.

> **Reading week.** Consolidation. Quiz revision begins.

los.title: Sprint 2 — Architecture as Inductive Bias → the Science Frontier
los.contentMd:
# Sprint 2 — Architecture as Inductive Bias → the Science Frontier

**Weeks 4–6.** One idea carries this sprint: an architecture is an assumption about the world. Week 4
establishes it for the standard model families; Week 5 takes it to its strongest form by building
physical law into the model itself. Week 6 consolidates everything so far.

## Week 4 — Model families: structure is an assumption about the world

`Indicative 4, 5` · `LO2, LO3` · `topic-04-model-families`

**Lecture (2h).** How connectivity yields capability — CNNs (spatial locality), RNNs and LSTMs
(sequence), transformers and attention (relations). The key idea carried into Week 5: an architecture
encodes assumptions about its data, and when those assumptions match reality, models need less data
and generalise better.

**Lab (2h).** Visualise what a CNN learns with the Convolution / Feature-Map Visualiser; explore
token relations with the Attention Visualiser.

## Week 5 — Science-inspired AI: building physical law into models

`Frontier — extends 4, 5` · `LO2` · `topic-05-science-inspired-ai`

**Lecture (2h).** Inductive bias drawn from science. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that
satisfy governing equations; neural operators (FNO, DeepONet) that learn PDE solution maps; neural
ODEs for continuous dynamics; equivariant and geometric deep learning (symmetry); diffusion models
understood as non-equilibrium thermodynamics; thermodynamics-informed GNNs. Why physical priors cut
data needs and improve reliability.

**Lab (2h).** Build a small PINN that solves an ODE or PDE — a damped oscillator, or the heat
equation — in the PINN Sandbox, and compare it against a data-only baseline for accuracy and data
efficiency.

## Week 6 — Quiz: foundations and the science frontier

`Assessment week` · `LO1, LO2, LO4, LO6` · `topic-06-quiz-and-review`

**Quiz (online, timed).** The first assessment piece, 50% of the module. Covers the history and
cycles of AI, classical ML and neural-network training, model families and frameworks, the
science-grounded architectures of Week 5, and the responsible-AI principles from Week 2. Full brief
in the Assessment unit.

**Lab (2h).** Structured pre-quiz review clinic: worked examples, concept-check exercises and a live
Q&A drawing the first five weeks together. The quiz is sat within, or immediately after, this session.

> **Reading week.** Consolidation; Sprint 3 preview.

los.title: Sprint 3 — LLMs, the Limits of Scale, and the Lean Turn
los.contentMd:
# Sprint 3 — LLMs, the Limits of Scale, and the Lean Turn

**Weeks 7–9.** The scaling era, then the two escapes from it: change the architecture so cost stops
being quadratic, or shrink the model until it runs on your own hardware.

## Week 7 — Transformers and LLMs: the scaling era and where it strains

`Indicative 5, 6, 7` · `LO3, LO4` · `topic-07-transformers-and-llms`

**Lecture (2h).** Transformer recap → LLMs: pretraining, fine-tuning, RLHF, tokenisation, emergent
ability. Open versus proprietary models — Llama, ChatGPT, DeepSeek. Then scaling laws and their
limits: diminishing returns, cost, energy, data ceilings. This motivates the lean turn that follows.

**Lab (2h).** Run LLMs locally with Ollama; use the Tokeniser Explorer; compare open and proprietary
models on the same prompts.

## Week 8 — Scale-free LLMs: beyond brute-force attention

`Frontier — extends 6, 7` · `LO3, LO7` · `topic-08-scale-free-llms`

**Lecture (2h).** The efficiency frontier. The quadratic-attention bottleneck → state-space models
(S4, Mamba, Mamba-2), RetNet, RWKV, and linear and attention-free architectures with constant memory
and linear-time inference. Mixture-of-experts and sparsity for capacity without cost.
Test-time-compute and reasoning models that scale inference rather than parameters.

**Lab (2h).** Run and benchmark a Mamba/SSM model against a comparable transformer; measure latency
and memory across sequence lengths with the Attention-vs-SSM Scaling Visualiser.

## Week 9 — Lean LLMs: small, cheap, private, on-device

`Frontier — extends 6, 7 + indicative 10` · `LO3, LO4, LO7` · `topic-09-lean-llms`

**Lecture (2h).** Making models lean: knowledge distillation, including transformer→recurrent
distillation; low-bit quantization from 4-bit down to 1-bit; pruning; and parameter-efficient
fine-tuning with LoRA and QLoRA. Small language models; edge and TinyML deployment; energy use and
neuromorphic/spiking approaches. Why lean matters — cost, privacy, sustainability, access.

**Lab (2h).** Quantize and LoRA-fine-tune a small model; deploy it under realistic edge constraints;
use the Compression Trade-off Explorer to weigh size against accuracy.

> **Reading week.** Final-project proposals released and reviewed. This is the proposal milestone —
> see the Assignment 2 brief.

los.title: Sprint 4 — Systems, Frontier Trends, Final Project
los.contentMd:
# Sprint 4 — Systems, Frontier Trends, Final Project

**Weeks 10–12.** From models to systems, then out to the frontier, then your own artefact.

## Week 10 — LLMs in software engineering and system design

`Indicative 8` · `LO5` · `topic-10-llms-in-software-engineering`

**Lecture (2h).** Agentic systems, AI-assisted development, retrieval-augmented generation,
embeddings and vector databases — and how to architect systems around lean local models plus frontier
APIs. The augmentation-not-replacement thesis, carried over from the Software Engineering
certificate.

**Lab (2h).** Build a RAG application powered by a local lean model; complete a real task with an AI
coding agent. Final-project build begins here.

## Week 11 — Frontier and emerging trends: from AI-for-science to the edge

`Indicative 10 + frontier` · `LO5, LO7` · `topic-11-frontier-trends`

**Lecture (2h).** AI as a scientific instrument leads the session — AlphaFold 2→3, GNoME materials
discovery, protein binder design, weather and climate models, science foundation models — with a
critical view that AI tends to complement rather than replace experimental work. Then the deployment
frontier: federated learning, edge AI, neuromorphic and spiking systems, quantum ML, agentic and
world models. How the science-inspired and lean currents are converging, and how to weigh substance
against hype.

**Lab (2h).** Explore an AI-predicted scientific structure with the Protein / Materials Explorer; run
a federated-learning or edge-ML demonstration. Continue the final-project build.

## Week 12 — Final project: build, showcase, reflect

`Assessment week` · `LO3, LO5, LO7` · `topic-12-final-project`

**Showcase (live).** The culminating assessment, 50% of the module. Present a working lean/LLM
artefact and a critical brief, followed by structured peer review. Full brief in the Assessment unit.

**Synthesis (closing).** A short wrap-up drawing the two frontier currents together — grounding
models in science, and shrinking them to run anywhere — and reflecting on the decade ahead.

> **Reading week.** Final-project submission.

los.contentMd:
# Reading

## Core texts

- **Russell, S. & Norvig, P. (2020)** *Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach.* The standard
  reference for the field's shape and history. Weeks 1 and 3.
- **Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y. & Courville, A. (2016)** *Deep Learning.* Training, optimisation and
  the model families. Weeks 3 and 4.
- **Bronstein, M. et al.** *Geometric Deep Learning.* Symmetry and equivariance as inductive bias —
  the theoretical backing for Week 5.

## Current literature

The frontier strands are too recent for textbooks. Reading for Weeks 5, 8, 9 and 11 is drawn from
current literature on **physics-informed machine learning**, **state-space models** and **model
compression**, and is refreshed each delivery to track the field.

> Per-week readings are posted in the relevant topic. Expect two or three papers a week in the
> frontier weeks, and expect at least one of them to have been published since the last delivery of
> this module.

## How to read the papers

You are not being asked to reproduce results. For each paper, be able to answer three questions:
what assumption about the data does this architecture encode, what does that assumption buy in data
efficiency or compute, and where does it break. That is also, not coincidentally, the shape of the
final-project brief.

# Week 1 Lab — orientation, and getting your tools working

AI Evolution Timeline as a macro orientation,
then environment setup for the remaining eleven weeks.

## Setup

```bash
bash setup.sh                    # macOS / Linux   (Windows: .\setup.ps1)
```

That creates the virtual environment, installs the **core** packages (small and
fast), and runs the environment check. When you have time and disk space before
Week 3, add the heavy stack:

```bash
bash setup.sh --full             # adds PyTorch, transformers, datasets, hf
```

Doing it by hand instead:

```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python setup_check.py            # never crashes; tells you what is missing
```

**`INSTALL.md` is the full guide** — Python per operating system, virtual
environments, Git and GitHub authentication, Colab, HuggingFace tokens and the
`hf` CLI, Ollama, and a troubleshooting table for the eight errors that actually
come up.

`setup_check.py` is the first thing to run and the thing to bring to the lab if
something is wrong. It reports on Python, the scientific stack, PyTorch and any
accelerator, HuggingFace, Ollama, git identity, and whether you are in Colab.

## The files

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `timeline_data.py` | 62 milestones, 1843–2025, each tagged with its **family** (symbolic / connectionist / statistical) and the **ingredient** it supplied. The dataset, not a picture of one. |
| `ai_timeline.py` | Four figures: the hype wave, the pendulum counted, the ingredient supply chart, and the era bands. Plus an ipywidgets year scrubber. |
| `three_ingredients.py` | The Week 1 thesis as a **runnable experiment**. No GPU, no download. |
| `setup_check.py` | Environment report card. |
| `hello_models.py` | First contact with HuggingFace and with Ollama. |
| `week1_lab.ipynb` | The guided version. |

los.title: Python
los.contentMd:
# Python

You need **3.11 or newer**. Check what you have:

```bash
python3 --version        # macOS / Linux
python --version         # Windows
```

If that fails or shows 3.10 or older:

- **Windows** — install from the Microsoft Store ("Python 3.12"), or python.org.
  On the python.org installer, **tick "Add python.exe to PATH"** on the first screen.
  Getting this wrong is the single most common cause of "python is not recognised".
- **macOS** — `brew install python@3.12`, or the python.org installer.
  Do **not** rely on the `/usr/bin/python3` that ships with macOS.
- **Linux** — `sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip` (Debian/Ubuntu).
  The `python3-venv` package is separate and is easy to miss.

### The rule that saves you a week of pain

> **Never `pip install` into your system Python.** Always work inside a virtual
> environment. When two modules need different versions of the same library —
> and they will — the venv is what stops them fighting.

los.title: The Virtual Environment
los.contentMd:
# The Virtual Environment

From inside this folder:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv                 # create it (once)

source .venv/bin/activate             # activate: macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate                # activate: Windows PowerShell

pip install -r requirements.txt       # install this module's packages
```

Your prompt should now start with `(.venv)`. That prefix is the whole point: it
tells you which Python you are about to run. If it disappears (new terminal
window, restarted editor), **activate again** — you have not broken anything.

To leave: `deactivate`.

There is a one-command version in `setup.sh` (macOS/Linux) and `setup.ps1`
(Windows) that does all of the above and then runs the environment check.

### If you prefer `uv`

`uv` is a much faster drop-in replacement and is fine to use here:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh    # macOS / Linux
uv venv && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt
```

# Git and GitHub

Your GitHub repository **is** the module deliverable. Every week adds to it, and
the Week 12 project is submitted from it.

```bash
git --version                         # install from git-scm.com if missing

git config --global user.name  "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@setu.ie"      # use your student address
```

Then, on github.com: **New repository** → name it something like
`ai-evolution-2026` → **Private** → Create. Follow the "push an existing
repository" instructions it shows you, or:

```bash
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Week 1: environment and timeline lab"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOURNAME/ai-evolution-2026.git
git push -u origin main
```

either:

- a **personal access token** (Settings → Developer settings → Tokens) pasted
  when git asks for a password, or
- the **GitHub CLI**: `gh auth login`, which handles it for you, or

  `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` into Settings → SSH keys.

los.title: HuggingFace
los.contentMd:
# HuggingFace

The Hub is where the models and datasets in Weeks 3 to 11 come from.

1. Create a free account at [huggingface.co](https://huggingface.co).
2. Settings → **Access Tokens** → New token → **Read** access is enough for now.
3. Log in from your machine:

```bash
pip install -U huggingface_hub
hf auth login              # paste the token when prompted
hf auth whoami             # confirms who you are
hf version
```

> The CLI used to be called `huggingface-cli`. It was renamed to `hf` in 2025.
> The old name still works but prints a deprecation warning; tutorials you find
> online will often still use it. `huggingface-cli login` == `hf auth login`.

Your first model:

```bash
python hello_models.py
```

**Where downloads go.** `~/.cache/huggingface` by default, and it gets large.
`hf cache scan` shows what is there; `hf cache delete` reclaims space. Set
`HF_HOME` to move it to another drive if your laptop is tight.

**Gated models.** Some (Llama, for instance) require you to accept a licence on
the model page while logged in. You will hit this in Week 7, not before.

los.title: Ollama
los.contentMd:
# Ollama

Ollama runs models **entirely on your own machine**: no API key, no account, and
no data leaving the laptop. It is the runtime behind Weeks 7 and 9, and the
single most persuasive demonstration of the lean turn in the whole module.

- **macOS / Windows** — download the installer from [ollama.com](https://ollama.com).
- **Linux** — `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`

Then:

```bash
ollama --version
ollama serve                      # starts the background service if not running
ollama pull llama3.2:1b           # about 1.3 GB — start small
ollama run llama3.2:1b "In two sentences, what was the AI winter of the 1970s?"
ollama list                       # what you have downloaded
```

It also exposes an HTTP API on `localhost:11434`, which is what `hello_models.py`
uses and what your Week 10 retrieval application will talk to:

```bash
curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{
  "model": "llama3.2:1b",
  "prompt": "Why did AlexNet matter?",
  "stream": false
}'
```

**Sizing.** A 1B model needs roughly 2 GB of RAM; 7–8B models need about 8 GB;
larger ones want a GPU. Start with `llama3.2:1b` and only go bigger if it is
comfortable.

los.title: When It Goes Wrong
los.contentMd:
# When It Goes Wrong

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `python: command not found` | Not on PATH, or it is `python3` on your system | Try `python3`. On Windows, reinstall ticking "Add to PATH" |
| `pip: externally-managed-environment` | You are installing into system Python | Activate the venv first. This error is the venv rule being enforced |

| `401 Unauthorized` from HuggingFace | Not logged in, or gated model | `hf auth login`, and accept the licence on the model page |
| Ollama: `connection refused` on 11434 | The service is not running | `ollama serve` in a separate terminal |
| Colab: "cannot connect to GPU backend" | Free tier is busy or your quota is used | Wait, or continue on CPU — Weeks 1–5 do not need a GPU |

# Submitting This Lab

Your submission is **one file**. A script in the lab folder builds it for you.

There is nothing to set up, no account to create, and no repository required.
It works the same way every week for the rest of the semester.

## The three steps

### 1. Answer the questions

Open `SUBMISSION.md` in the lab folder. Fill in your student number, your
name, and the answers to this week's exercises.

Delete each `TODO` marker as you finish that section.

### 2. Build your submission

In the lab folder, with your virtual environment active:

```bash
python make_submission.py
```

It will ask for your student number the first time and remember it afterwards.

The script checks your work, runs `setup_check.py`, gathers your files, and
produces a single zip named after you:

```
submission-week01-20012345.zip
```

It tells you exactly where that file is when it finishes.

**If it stops instead**, read the message. It stops for one reason only: your
`SUBMISSION.md` still has `TODO` markers in it, which means it is not
finished. Finish it and run the script again.

### 3. Upload it

**[Upload your Week 1 submission here](https://forms.cloud.microsoft/Pages/DesignPageV2.aspx?origin=NeoPortalPage&subpage=design&id=OcL4BRfLVUejRQSHUgY8Owb1PJvAbX9FgujLMW5Z7VpUM1E5SkpSMTVSNDNSSFVCNTFPQzVPMkhCTi4u&analysis=false)**

**[Submission Option 2](https://setuo365-my.sharepoint.com/:f:/g/personal/indrakshi_dey_setu_ie/IgCwbDLbNP_YTKcfdSFcRKqtAX7FawPZq6RGiLrI6t1Wne4)**

Upload that one zip. Nothing else. Do not upload individual files, do not
email them, and do not upload a folder.

That is the whole submission.

## What is in the file

You can open the zip and look — there are no surprises in it:

| Inside the zip | What it is |
|---|---|
| `SUBMISSION.md` | Your answers |
| Any images you saved | Your plots |
| `submission/` | Anything else you chose to include |
| `setup_check_output.txt` | Your environment report, captured automatically |
| `manifest.json` | Your student number, the week, and a timestamp |

Nothing is sent anywhere. The script runs entirely on your machine and only
writes a file.

## Common problems

**"It says my SUBMISSION.md is not finished."**
There is still a `TODO` in it. Search for the word and answer that section.

**"I need to submit even though it is incomplete."**
You can, and sometimes that is the right call:

```bash
python make_submission.py --force
```

It will be recorded as incomplete, which is better than not being recorded
at all.

**"It could not work out which week this is."**
Tell it:

```bash
python make_submission.py --week 1
```

**"I typed my student number wrong."**
Delete the file `.student_number` in the lab folder and run the script again.

**"I already uploaded and then fixed something."**
Upload again. The latest upload is the one that counts.

## Anything else to add

If you want to include extra work — a notebook, some notes, a second plot —
make a folder called `submission` inside the lab folder and put them there.
Everything in it goes into the zip.

## Deadlines and marks

Weekly labs are **pass/fail completion checkpoints**. No single one carries a
mark. They exist so that you and I both know, every week, whether you are
keeping up.

Deadlines are **23:59 on the Sunday after each lab**. Late still counts as
submitted; it is simply recorded as late.

The Week 6 quiz and the Week 12 project are submitted separately and are the
things that carry marks.

## If you are stuck

There are no lab tutors on this module, so the order matters.

1. **The troubleshooting table in `INSTALL.md`.** Eight errors, and between
   them they cover most of what actually goes wrong. Check it first.
2. **The module channel.** Post there rather than emailing me — someone else
   has the same problem, and the answer helps everyone reading. Include the
   output of `python setup_check.py`, not "it doesn't work".
3. **Email me.** Expect a reply within two working days.

Getting stuck on environment setup is completely normal and says nothing about
your ability. Getting stuck silently for three weeks is the only version that
causes real damage.

# Step 1 · Meet the data

*≈ 20 min · lecture: pipeline stages World → Data → Labels*

## What you are doing

The lecture said: **the world is the first dataset, and it is not fair.** Here you look
at the loan file before any model is trained. Each person has seven "permitted" facts
(income, savings, postcode score, ...) and an outcome column `repaid`.

## Run this

The first cell of the notebook loads everything. The second is Step 1:

```python
df = lab["df"]
h.describe_mechanisms(df)                               # Printout A
print(df.groupby("group").latent.mean().round(3))      # Printout B: true ability, by group

h.population_table(df)[["group", "n", "share", "repaid_rate", "mean_income",
                        "mean_savings", "mean_credit_history_months",
                        "mean_postcode_score"]].round(3)
```

## What you should see

- **Printout A:** the four mechanisms, each with its pipeline stage and one line on what it did:

```
  [x] sampling_bias     Data     group B is only about 20% of the file, not 50%
  [x] historical_bias   World    at equal ability, B has lower recorded income and savings ...
  [x] proxy             Data     postcode_score almost perfectly reveals which group someone is in
  [x] label_bias        Labels   some group B people who repaid were recorded as defaulting
```

- **Printout B:** two "true ability" numbers that are almost identical (about `-0.017` and `-0.005`).
  **That is the proof the groups are equal.**
- **Table C**, the population table:

| group | n | share | repaid_rate | mean_income | mean_savings | mean_credit_history_months | mean_postcode_score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 6372 | 0.796 | 0.547 | 31,840 | 4,197 | 83.5 | 0.717 |
| B | 1628 | 0.204 | 0.437 | 25,756 | 2,333 | 53.6 | 0.064 |

On paper, group B is a fifth of the file, earns less, has saved less, has a shorter
credit history, and repays eleven points less often. In reality B is equal. Everything
"on paper" was put there by the mechanisms.

## Check these against `SUBMISSION.md`, Step 1

- **1a.** What share of the dataset is group B?
  *Where to look: Table C, row B, column `share`.*
- **1b.** The recorded repayment rate for A, and for B.
  *Where to look: Table C, column `repaid_rate`.*
- **1c.** The groups are *equally* able to repay. So is the difference in 1b caused by
  **ability** or by **how the data was made**? (one word)
  *Where to look: Printout B shows the abilities are equal; Printout A lists what made the difference.*
- **1d.** "Some group B people who repaid were recorded as defaulting" belongs to which
  pipeline stage: **World, Data, or Labels**?
  *Where to look: Printout A, the `label_bias` line. That sentence is printed there with its stage.*

That is Step 1 done.

los.title: Step 2 · Does hiding `group` fix it?
los.contentMd:
# Step 2 · Does hiding `group` fix it?

*≈ 15 min · lecture: "fairness through unawareness"*

## What you are doing

The most common "fix" anyone suggests: *just don't give the model the `group` column.*
The lecture called this **fairness through unawareness** and said it does not work,
because other columns **leak** the group.

Test it: train a throw-away model to *guess* someone's group using **only** the seven
permitted columns. If it can guess well, the group was never hidden.

## Run this

```python
from datasets import proxy_recoverability
rec = proxy_recoverability(df)
print(f"Line A: guessing `group` from permitted columns: {rec.attrs['accuracy']:.1%}")
print(f"Line B: just guessing 'A' every time:            {rec.attrs['majority_baseline']:.1%}")
rec.round(4)
```

## What you should see

```
Line A: guessing `group` from permitted columns: 99.6%
Line B: just guessing 'A' every time:            79.6%

feature                 importance
postcode_score              0.3260
savings                     0.0008
existing_debt               0.0005
...
```

One column with a huge importance and the rest near zero. That column is the **proxy**.
The attribute you refused to record is recoverable at 99.6%, and you have not even
trained the lending model yet.

## Check these against `SUBMISSION.md`, Step 2

- **2a.** The accuracy of guessing `group` from the permitted columns.
  *Where to look: Line A.*
- **2b.** The column that leaks the group.
  *Where to look: the table, top row (biggest importance).*
- **2c.** One sentence: why does deleting the `group` column *not* stop the model treating
  the groups differently?
  *Where to look: 2a and 2b are the whole answer.*

That is Step 2 done.

los.title: Step 3 · The model, and the line you draw
los.contentMd:
# Step 3 · The model, and the line you draw

*≈ 25 min · lecture: pipeline stages Model → Threshold, "where you cut"*

## What you are doing

A standard, well-built model has already been trained for you. It never saw `group`.
For each applicant it gives a **score** between 0 and 1: how likely they are to repay.
You then choose a **threshold**: approve everyone above the line, refuse everyone below.

The lecture said: **the threshold is one number, and it decides who bears every error.**

Four numbers appear per group:

| number | meaning |
|---|---|
| approval rate | share of the group that gets a loan |
| accuracy | share of decisions that were right |
| TPR | share of *good* borrowers who were (correctly) approved |
| FPR | share of *bad* borrowers who were (wrongly) approved |

## Run this

```python
h.try_threshold(lab, 0.5)
```

## What you should see

```
threshold 0.50   approval rate overall 55.4%   gap in approval rate between groups 0.203

group     n   approval rate   accuracy   TPR    FPR
A      2230           0.596      0.706  0.776  0.378
B       570           0.393      0.668  0.570  0.255
```

Group A is approved about **60%** of the time, group B about **39%**: a gap of **twenty
points** between two groups that are equally able to repay. Good borrowers in A are
approved 78% of the time; in B, 57%.

Now the picture:

```python
ex.fig_distributions(lab["y"], lab["scores"], lab["group"], 0.5); plt.show()
```

![Two hills, one line](img/distributions.png)

Group B's hill sits to the **left**, so the same line cuts off more of B. Nothing about
the model is "wrong"; it learned the manufactured data faithfully.

## Move the line

Change the number and run again. Try `0.3`, `0.4`, `0.6`:

```python
h.try_threshold(lab, 0.4)
```

## The "perfectly fair" line that helps nobody

```python
h.find_equal_approval_threshold(lab)
```

```
threshold   gap in approval rate   approval rate overall   accuracy
     0.98                  0.024                   0.019      0.489
     0.02                  0.032                   0.990      0.532
```

The gap only disappears at thresholds that approve **2%** of everyone, or **99%** of
everyone. The gap is "fair" because almost nobody, or almost everybody, gets a loan.
**A fairness number quoted without the approval rate is meaningless.**

## Check these against `SUBMISSION.md`, Step 3

- **3a.** At threshold 0.5: approval rate for A, for B, and the gap.
  *Where to look: the `try_threshold(lab, 0.5)` output: rows A and B, column `approval rate`; the gap is on the first printed line.*
- **3b.** One other threshold you tried: its gap and its overall approval rate.
  *Where to look: the first printed line of your own `try_threshold` run.*
- **3c.** At the threshold with the smallest gap (0.98), what share of people get a loan?
  *Where to look: the `find_equal_approval_threshold` table, top row, column `approval rate overall`.*
- **3d.** One sentence: why must a fairness number always be reported **together with**
  the approval rate?
  *Where to look: 3c is the evidence.*

That is Step 3 done.

los.title: Step 4 · Four fixes, and what each one costs
los.contentMd:
# Step 4 · Four fixes, and what each one costs

*≈ 20 min · lecture: "fairness is not a feature you add; it is a set of choices you already made"*

## What you are doing

Now try to close the gap. Four ideas from the lecture, one table:

1. **Drop the proxy column** (`postcode_score`): remove the leak.
2. **Reweight the training data** so group B counts as much as group A.
3. **Different thresholds per group**: tune the line separately for A and B until one gap is zero.
4. **Fix the labels**: go back to pipeline stage *Labels* and use the correct repayment records.

## Run this (about 20 seconds)

```python
fixes = mitigate.compare_all(n=8000, seed=1)
fixes.drop(columns=["thresholds"]).round(3)
```

## What you should see

| strategy | accuracy | selection_gap | tpr_gap | fpr_gap | ppv_gap | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline (nothing done) | 0.699 | 0.203 | 0.205 | 0.122 | 0.079 | |
| drop postcode_score | 0.684 | **0.273** | 0.273 | 0.202 | 0.046 | ← worse |
| reweighting (pre) | 0.682 | 0.103 | 0.115 | 0.020 | 0.126 | |
| per-group thresholds (selection_gap) | 0.684 | **0.000** | 0.030 | 0.098 | **0.163** | ← one gap zero, another up |
| per-group thresholds (fpr_gap) | 0.689 | 0.085 | 0.094 | 0.001 | 0.130 | |
| fix the label (stage 3) | 0.698 | **0.033** | 0.033 | 0.032 | 0.009 | ← best, and no accuracy lost |

`selection_gap` is the approval-rate gap from Step 3. Read the table top to bottom:

- Dropping the proxy makes the gap **bigger**. The model leans harder on the other leaky columns.
- Reweighting helps a bit and costs a bit of accuracy.
- Per-group thresholds zero the gap you tuned for and **push another gap up**. You cannot
  have every gap at zero at once; the lecture called this the impossibility result.
- **Fixing the label** removes nearly all of it and costs almost nothing, because that is
  **where the harm was put in**. The cheapest real fix is the earliest one.

## Check these against `SUBMISSION.md`, Step 4

- **4a.** Which fix made the approval gap **worse**?
  *Where to look: column `selection_gap`, the only row bigger than the baseline's 0.203.*
- **4b.** Which fix got the gap to exactly 0.000, and which *other* gap went up when it did?
  *Where to look: the row with `selection_gap` 0.000; read across to `ppv_gap` and compare with the baseline row.*
- **4c.** Which fix worked best overall, and how much accuracy did it cost?
  *Where to look: the last row; column `accuracy`, compared with the baseline row.*
- **4d.** One sentence: why did fixing the *label* work better than fixing the *model*?
  *Where to look: Step 1, Printout A: `label_bias` is a Labels-stage mechanism, so the fix at the Labels stage removes it at source.*

That is Step 4 done.

los.title: Going Further (optional)
los.contentMd:
# Going Further (optional)

Everything here is for people who finished the five steps and want more. Each is one cell
in the notebook.

## A. Which mechanism did the damage?

```python
h.mechanism_table()
```

| mechanism switched on | gap in approval rate | gap in TPR | accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| none (clean data) | 0.003 | 0.013 | 0.693 |
| sampling_bias | 0.005 | 0.011 | 0.686 |
| historical_bias | **0.148** | 0.156 | 0.674 |
| proxy | 0.004 | 0.018 | 0.693 |
| label_bias | 0.018 | 0.035 | **0.662** |
| all four | 0.203 | 0.205 | 0.699 |

Historical disadvantage alone produces most of the gap. Biased labels alone hurt
*accuracy* most. The proxy alone does nothing, until another mechanism gives it something
to leak. Different mechanisms hurt different metrics; that is why the lecture's pipeline
has seven stops, not one.

## B. The impossibility table

```python
fig, table = ex.fig_impossibility(lab["y"], lab["scores"], lab["group"]); plt.show()
table.round(3)
```

![Each row zeroes one gap; read across the row](img/impossibility.png)

Each row tunes per-group thresholds to zero **one** gap. The other gaps do not follow.
No row zeroes all three, because no such thresholds exist.

## C. Explain one refused applicant

```python
import explain
from datasets import FEATURES
refused = lab["test"][(lab["scores"] < 0.4) & (lab["test"].group == "B")].index[0]
local = explain.lime_from_scratch(lab["model"], lab["train"][FEATURES], lab["test"].loc[refused, FEATURES])
explain.fig_local_explanation(local); plt.show()
```

An explanation tells you what the model **used**. It does not tell you whether it
**should** have. `postcode_score` barely appears, yet Step 2 showed it carries the group.

## D. A simpler model

```python
pd.concat([h.worst_group_accuracy(lab, "gbm"), h.worst_group_accuracy(lab, "logreg")])
```

Compare accuracy **per group**, not the headline. The Week 9 preview.

## E. The full templates

`model_card_template_full.md` (Mitchell et al.) and `datasheet_template.md` (Gebru et
al.) are the blank professional long forms. The completed short `model_card.md` and
`datasheet.md` in the folder are the format the Week 12 project uses.

# Exercise 1 · A formula with dials

*≈ 20 min · lecture Part 1, slides 6 to 11*

## From the lecture

> **Red box 1:** *A model is a formula with dials. Learning is turning the dials so the guesses
> match the answers. The loop is Guess → Check → Blame → Nudge, repeated. Parameters are learned
> by the computer; hyperparameters are chosen by you.*

## What you are doing

Slide 7 used a house-price formula: **price = a × size + b**. Here are five houses. You set the
two dials **a** and **b** by hand and see every guess and its miss. Then you hand the dials to the
computer and watch it go round the four-step loop from slide 8, one trip per row. Then thousands
of trips, and the model reads as a sentence.

## Run this

```python
ls.house_dials(a=2.0, b=50)      # change a and b, run again. Try a=3, b=0.
```

## What you should see

  CHECK: target 1.0, loss = 0.5 x (0.626 - 1.0)^2 = 0.070
